chapter: Detroit 1927: Pollack, Casa Loma, Atlantic City
title: Trip to Chicago to hear Ben Pollack and Benny Goodman
summary: The Goldkette men drove to Chicago to hear Pollack's band, especially the drum and clarinet feature with Goodman.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: Had you heard them on record?
But you hadn't seen them in person.

I hadn't, but now we -- Trumbauer got this up. He said, 'We'll go sometime, let's go out to Chicago and hear Pollack, who was playing then at this place called the Southmore Hotel and I think he had made some records with the Williams Sisters and they were from Scranton, by the way, right outside of Scranton and I had worked with them. When I was home.

Anyway, so we decided to go. It was quite a trip. Trumbauer had a car, we got his wife and son and Bix and I and we had maybe Bill Rank. We had some guys in there and we decided to go out and listen to the band. Well, it was around dark when we got there, and Trumbauer seemed to know his way around. I hadn't been to Chicago, so they found the place, found the hotel when it was the proper time and we went up and
listened to the band. They played all of their goodies for us. There was Ben Pollack and Benny Goodman.
Did he play drums or did he front the band?

No, he played drums then. Fantastic drummer. "99 to the Bar," he used to tell us, but he was -- they had a feature that they used to do that knocked us out. They'd go along playing a tune you know, and play their choruses and this guy would play his chorus and that guy would play his chorus, and then they'd come to Benny's chorus and the rest of the band would drop out and it would be just drums and clarinet. My God, it was real -- it was great.
Of course, then Benny did it with Krupa later on in his own band.
He did? I never heard him do that.
Well, I mean, 'Sing, Sing, Sing,' the whole thing with the clarinet and the drums, that portion of Sing, Sing, Sing.

I'm not familiar with that. But they did it a couple of times and I remember later on when I was with the Whiteman band, they came to New York and played in a place called the Little Club and they did the same thing there, and you know, it went unappreciated. It was discouraging to see some things come along like that and not have somebody there to appreciate it, only a couple of musicians sitting around.

But they did that to perfection. You could tell all the harmony and Benny would come out with all the harmonies, you know, you listen to him, you knew what the harmonies were that he was playing, and you knew what the harmony of the tune was he was playing. And Pollack, he was a great drummer, he really was.
